questions.q: What does the lesson suggest as a good way to measure the potential harm of a generative AI application?
options: Measuring how fast the model answers
Counting how many users sign up
Testing a diverse set of prompts that users are most likely to use
Asking the model whether it is harmful
questions.explain: Builders should keep a wide, diverse user base in mind and test the prompts real users will send.
questions.evidence: testing a diverse set of prompts users are most likely going to use is a good way to measure potential harm.

questions.q: What is ethics based on, according to the data ethics lesson?
options: Widely accepted norms of what is right versus wrong, not laws
The laws of each country only
The terms of service of software products
Personal preferences of developers
questions.explain: Laws set minimum requirements; ethics is about shared norms, which organisations operationalise through an ethics culture.
questions.evidence: Ethics is based not on laws but on widely accepted norms of what is "right vs. wrong".

questions.q: When does selection bias occur?
options: When a model is too large
When labels are written by experts
When features are scaled
When a dataset's examples are chosen in a way that does not reflect their real-world distribution
questions.explain: If the sample is unrepresentative, the model learns a distorted picture of the world.
questions.evidence: Selection bias occurs if a dataset's examples are chosen in a way that is not reflective of their real-world distribution.

questions.q: How does the NIST AI RMF describe risk tolerance?
options: A fixed threshold set by NIST for all AI systems
Highly contextual and specific to the application and use case
Irrelevant once a system is deployed
The same for every organisation in a sector
questions.explain: What level of risk is acceptable depends on context, so the framework does not prescribe one.
questions.evidence: Risk tolerance and the level of risk that is acceptable to organizations or society are highly contextual and application and use-case specific.

questions.q: Which trustworthiness characteristic does the NIST AI RMF show as the base for all the others?
options: Privacy-enhanced
Explainable and interpretable
Valid and reliable
Fair, with harmful bias managed
questions.explain: A system that is not valid and reliable cannot be trustworthy in any other respect.
questions.evidence: Valid & Reliable is a necessary condition of trustworthiness and is shown as the base for other trustworthiness characteristics.

questions.q: Under 'Govern 2' of the AI RMF Core, what must be in place?
options: A budget for buying AI tools
A public list of all training data
A ban on third-party models
Accountability structures so the right teams and people are empowered, responsible and trained to map, measure and manage AI risks
questions.explain: Governance is about clear roles and responsibilities for managing AI risk.
questions.evidence: Govern 2: Accountability structures are in place so that the appropriate teams and individuals are empowered, responsible, and trained for mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks.

questions.q: Which is a way AI risks differ from traditional software risks?
options: Training data may become detached from its intended context or outdated relative to the deployment context
AI systems never need testing
AI systems cannot be attacked
AI systems always explain their decisions
questions.explain: Data-driven behaviour can drift as the world changes, which traditional code does not.
questions.evidence: Datasets used to train AI systems may become detached from their original and intended context or may become stale or outdated relative to deployment context.

questions.q: Why should you take particular care with algorithms used where there are known historical inequalities?
options: Because such algorithms run more slowly
Because the available training data is likely to encode the same biases
Because the law forbids them
Because their results cannot be explained
questions.explain: Historical data reflects historical unfairness, which a model will learn unless you correct for it.
questions.evidence: as the available training data is likely to encode these same biases.

questions.q: Which privacy principle does the Data and AI Ethics Framework recommend upholding?
options: Collect as much data as possible in case it is useful later
Only tell users about data use if they ask
Nobody should be surprised about how their data is being used
Personal data can be used freely inside government
questions.explain: Explain what you collect, why, how it is used and how long it is kept.
questions.evidence: A good principle to uphold is that nobody should be surprised about how their data is being used.

questions.q: What does responsible AI refer to?
options: Using AI only for research
AI that has passed a government licence exam
AI systems that cannot make mistakes
Developing and using AI in a way that is ethical, transparent and aligned with societal values
questions.explain: It covers fairness, privacy, robustness, transparency and accountability across the AI lifecycle.
questions.evidence: Responsible AI refers to the development and use of artificial intelligence in a way that is ethical, transparent, and aligns with societal values.

questions.q: A sentiment model trained mostly on reviews from people who loved or hated a book struggles with subtle reviews. Which bias explains this?
options: Reporting bias
In-group bias
Automation bias
Experimenter's bias
questions.explain: People mostly write reviews when they feel strongly, so the data doesn't reflect how often moderate opinions occur.
questions.evidence: Reporting bias occurs when the frequency of events, properties, and/or outcomes captured in a dataset does not accurately reflect their real-world frequency.

questions.q: A surveyor uses the first 200 consumers who answered an email instead of a random sample. Which bias is this?
options: Coverage bias
Sampling bias
Reporting bias
Out-group homogeneity bias
questions.explain: Early responders may be more enthusiastic than average buyers; proper randomisation avoids this.
questions.evidence: Sampling bias occurs if proper randomization is not used during data collection.

questions.q: What is coverage bias?
options: Training a model until it confirms your hypothesis
Favouring automated results over human ones
Data that is not selected in a representative way
Stereotyping members of other groups
questions.explain: Coverage bias is a kind of selection bias: some parts of the population are missing from the data.
questions.evidence: Coverage bias occurs if data is not selected in a representative fashion.

questions.q: What is automation bias?
options: Automating data collection without consent
Favouring results from automated systems regardless of their error rates
Preferring people from your own group
Collecting data without randomisation
questions.explain: People tend to trust a machine's output even when a human method is more accurate.
questions.evidence: Automation bias is a tendency to favor results generated by automated systems over those generated by non-automated systems, irrespective of the error rates of each.

questions.q: A model builder keeps training until the model produces the result they expected. Which bias is this?
options: Experimenter's bias
Coverage bias
Reporting bias
Group attribution bias
questions.explain: Stopping only when results match the original hypothesis bakes that belief into the model.
questions.evidence: Experimenter's bias occurs when a model builder keeps training a model until it produces a result that aligns with their original hypothesis.

questions.q: What is out-group homogeneity bias?
options: Preferring members of your own group
Generalising one person's traits to their whole group
Ignoring rare events in the data
Seeing members of groups you don't belong to as more alike than they are
questions.explain: It stereotypes individuals of other groups and treats their characteristics as uniform.
questions.evidence: or to see their characteristics as more uniform

questions.q: According to the NIST AI RMF, how strong is a system's trustworthiness?
options: As strong as its strongest characteristic
Fixed once the system is certified
Only as strong as its weakest characteristic
Determined by accuracy alone
questions.explain: Trustworthiness is a social concept on a spectrum; trade-offs between characteristics must be justified.
questions.evidence: is only as strong as its weakest characteristics

questions.q: Why is 'Accountable & Transparent' drawn as a vertical box in the NIST trustworthiness diagram?
options: It is the least important characteristic
It relates to all the other characteristics
It applies only to AI vendors
It is optional for low-risk systems
questions.explain: Valid & Reliable forms the base; accountability and transparency cut across everything else.
questions.evidence: Accountable & Transparent is shown as a vertical box because it relates to all other characteristics.

questions.q: In the AI RMF, what are 'negative residual risks'?
options: The sum of all unmitigated risks
Risks that have been fully removed
Risks accepted by a regulator
Risks found only after deployment
questions.explain: Manage 1.4 asks for them to be documented for downstream acquirers and end users.
questions.evidence: Negative residual risks (defined as the sum of all unmitigated risks)

questions.q: How should a team use the Data and AI Ethics Framework during a project?
options: Read it once at the start
Use it only after deployment
Complete it as a one-off checklist
Revisit it regularly, especially when the work changes
questions.explain: It is meant to guide decisions across the whole life cycle, alongside the self-assessment tool.
questions.evidence: You should regularly revisit it throughout your project, especially when you make changes to your work or project.

questions.q: What is 'process transparency' in the Data and AI Ethics Framework?
options: Publishing the model's source code
Making all the training data open
Information about the design, development and deployment decisions behind the AI
Showing users the model's accuracy score
questions.explain: Technical transparency covers code and data; process transparency covers how and why decisions were made.
questions.evidence: Process transparency This is information about the design, development and deployment decisions and practices behind your AI solutions

questions.q: What does accountability mean when a data or AI system harms someone?
options: The user has to accept the risk
The harm can be raised and fixed
The system is switched off permanently
Nobody is responsible because the AI decided
questions.explain: Accountability also means clear roles and responsibilities at every stage of the project.
questions.evidence: if something goes wrong and a system or process harms someone, this can be raised and fixed

questions.q: Why should environmental sustainability be considered from the very start of a project?
options: It can shape your choices of tools, suppliers and infrastructure
It is only checked by auditors at the end
It only matters for hardware projects
It is a legal formality with no design impact
questions.explain: Early choices about compute and suppliers fix much of a project's environmental footprint.
questions.evidence: as it can influence your choices about tools, suppliers and infrastructure

questions.q: What does 'societal impact' refer to in the framework?
options: The media coverage a project receives
The number of people who use a system
The cost savings from automation
The effects data and AI can have on individuals, communities, social structures and economies
questions.explain: Understanding it requires knowing the social and technical context a system is used in.
questions.evidence: Societal impact refers to the effects that data and AI can have on individuals, communities, social structures and economies.

questions.q: In the context of data-driven technologies, which themes does 'safety' cover?
options: Speed, cost, popularity and scale
Colour, layout, fonts and branding
Accuracy, security, reliability and robustness
Profit, growth, market share and reach
questions.explain: Safety matters most in high-risk areas such as healthcare, policing and justice.
questions.evidence: safety refers to themes such as accuracy, security, reliability and robustness

questions.q: Why do AI systems often have larger attack surfaces than traditional systems?
options: They always run on public clouds
They rely on data and models as well as software
They open more network ports
They are usually written in Python
questions.explain: Training data, models and algorithms are all new targets for attackers.
questions.evidence: This is because they not only rely on software but also on data and models.

questions.q: Which threat is specific to AI systems rather than traditional cybersecurity?
options: Targeting the training data to manipulate the model
Phishing emails
Malware on laptops
Network intrusions
questions.explain: Traditional cybersecurity mainly deals with malware, phishing and network intrusions.
questions.evidence: Attackers can target the training data, manipulate models, or exploit vulnerabilities in the algorithms themselves.

questions.q: Why does limited interpretability make AI systems harder to secure?
options: AI systems never record their decisions
Humans cannot read AI source code
AI models are always open source
It is harder to understand why the system made a particular decision
questions.explain: If you cannot explain a decision, it is harder to tell a manipulated output from a normal one.
questions.evidence: Understanding why an AI system made a particular decision is often more challenging compared to traditional software systems.

questions.q: How do privacy and data protection link responsible AI and AI security?
options: Responsible AI forbids security testing
Privacy only matters for marketing teams
Respecting privacy and securing personal data is part of responsible AI
Security teams decide what counts as ethical
questions.explain: Ethical considerations such as privacy directly affect how an AI system must be secured.
questions.evidence: Ensuring that AI systems respect user privacy and secure personal data is a key aspect of responsible AI.

questions.q: Which principle is core to both responsible AI and AI security?
options: Maximising model size
Robustness against manipulation and attacks
Keeping every model secret
Training only on open data
questions.explain: This includes defending against adversarial attacks and protecting the integrity of decisions.
questions.evidence: AI systems must be robust against manipulation and attacks, which is a core principle of both responsible AI and AI security.
